object_description: simple flat two-storey structure filling the site around a large open entrance courtyard
geometry_property: concrete skeleton behind a timber column facade
design_condition: the flat volume is set back slightly from the avenue and extends between its two mighty neighbours over the whole available land, oriented entirely to the main access axis with its ground floor raised about a metre

positive: The simple flat structure is fully oriented towards the important access axis of the avenue
The inviting design of the entrance area partially makes up for the lack of outdoor space
A large open courtyard brings all entrances together very clearly and forms the centre of the department
The entrance courtyard is accessed via a wide and inviting ramp
Seating steps in the inner courtyard ensure a pleasant quality of stay with a student atmosphere
Thanks to the open entrance courtyard both entrance areas and the reception are attractive and well lit
Respecting the narrower perimeter creates a generous front zone allowing the second tree row to continue
The individual functional areas are well separated in the building
The flexible concrete skeleton structure allows a clear organisation
The narrow facade grid, wooden infills and textile sun protection give a restrained, elegant appearance
Operational synergies from a shared counter for reception, secretariat and library are welcomed
Access to and organisation of the sports hall works well
The construction is easy to read for all components and therefore easy to calculate
The proportion of glazing is reduced to what is necessary, an advantage for the energy standard
In the quiet two-storey structure the central entrance courtyard provides good lighting and orientation
negative: The potential of the courtyard is not fully exploited internally, as the main staircase is spatially unappealing
Access to the large lecture hall is confusing and narrow
The gymnastics hall sits lower than the ground floor and has to do without an internal connection
Access leads directly into the hall without a vestibule
The choice of materials and appearance is questioned for this building task
The gained front zones are almost completely overlaid with bicycle parking, significantly impairing the appearance
The retained avenue fragment is not integrated spatially or functionally and degenerates into residual space
Interesting open space themes are clearly flawed in their implementation
The reception and waiting area on the upper floor is not very practical and patient flow is awkward
Some rooms are unfavourably proportioned and an intermediate preparation and quiet room is missing
Orientation in the building needs improvement, especially the location of the lecture hall
Offices are accessed via complicated routes through the patient area
Dispensing with a western entrance leaves the space between the buildings without recreational quality
Raising the ground floor by a metre brings hardly any discernible advantages and creates an unnecessary obstacle
Additional ramps are either too steep or need redesign for approval
Group rooms are only reachable inside via steps and the level differences hinder deliveries
The ramp in the courtyard costs the lecture hall below a reasonable spatial geometry
The upper entrance only makes sense as a secondary entrance, leading into an unattractive corridor
Converting the open-space area into group offices is difficult due to the large room depth
Considerable waiting times may occur at the shared counter during rush hours
Front zones to lecture hall and seminar rooms are insufficiently dimensioned and the stepped lecture hall ceiling is unsuitable for projection
The cafeteria is too peripheral as a meeting point and centre of the department
Deliveries have to be made via the main entrance and the kitchen workstations are insufficiently lit
Student lockers are distributed through laboratory and office areas where no students will spend time
Sealing the building off completely from the western exterior space is questioned
